title: Fantasy Premier League
text:
The Beautiful Game
This is my journey of playing FPL with 0 ball knowledge and a bit of Python knowledge.

WeeklyCumulative

























To counteract that I don’t know who I would’ve captained in my initial squad each week, I’m including the bench. This seems roughly fair. If I can beat the initial 15 line, that feels like a win.

title: Preseason
text:
The Goal
The purpose of this project is to see how well I can perform using a systematic set of trading rules based on historical data, rather than any knowledge or experience of football

title: Preseason
text:
The Goalposts
What does “performing well” mean? The most natural measure of performance is percentile rank among all FPL players, but that doesn’t have an objective benchmark. Is 50% good? 33%?
Perhaps the most objective measure of my performance is the difference between my final point score and the score I would have ended on if I had made no transfers throughout the season. This will evaluate the quality of my transfer decisions, but not of my initial choice of squad. I think I am happy with this, because I expect my initial squad to be far from both the best and worst initial squad.
Since my evaluation method is essentially controlling for the initial squad choice, once the season is over I might be able to work out how well my initial squad would have done with 0 transfers, compared to all the other possibilities.

title: Preseason
text:
Relegation zone
That leaves me with a baseline target of ensuring my final points is higher than the points my initial squad would have ended up on. With 37 transfers

title: Preseason
text:
Promotion zone
A target that feels certainly ambitious and objective (although, impossible to gauge if at all realistic) target might be to end on more than 1.5x the points that my initial squad would have

title: Preseason
text:
Safe zone
Ending up in the Relegation Zone will be an embarrassing but fun story to tell. Ending up in the Promotion Zone will be an even more fun story to tell. If both elude me, then at least I will have the code for my CV.

title: Preseason
text:
Formation
How should I choose when to buy, sell, and hold players? And on the basis of what data? I will be using moving averages to make my decisions. I will aim to buy players who are perform well over the last 3 weeks, and vice versa for selling. I will not waste my transfers transacting on averagely performing players, meaning I might not buy good players who are not good enough, and might not sell (i.e. will hold) players who are not (yet) performing badly enough.

title: Preseason
text:
Financial fairplay
I will only be using data available from the official FPL API. More specifically, I’ll only be using data pertaining to players’ points scored in the current and past two seasons. I will not make any decisions based on qualitative or other quantitative data I receive in any form or via any means, external to the API. Secondarily, this means I am not “cheating”. Primarily, this is because I have no reason to believe I’ll be able to employ this information better than that from the API.

title: Preseason
text:
Pitch limits
Currently undecided if I want to use chips. I think if I do, I will resign myself to using them the week before they expire, or not at all, on the basis that if I am going to use them, I should use them when I have the most information to hand. But, I don’t think I’ll use them, because it’ll make it very difficult to compare my performance with my initial squad’s. I would have to work out how I would have used them, had I kept my initial squad, which feels like a lot of work.

title: GW 1: The Initial Squad
text:
The Initial Squad
Before I choose which players I want, how do I choose how many of each position I want, subject to the maximum constraints? I’ll decide based on the average points scored for each position, over the last season:


Mean Goalkeeper Points over last season: 72
Mean Defender Points over last season: 74
Mean Midfielder Points over last season: 70
Mean Forward Points over last season: 70
Mean Goalkeeper cost: 4.7
Mean Defender cost: 4.8
Mean Midfielder cost: 5.6
Mean Forward cost: 6.0


So, very crudely, Defenders are a bit more lucrative than other positions, and the opposite for Forwards. So I’ll pick two Goalkeeprs, then as many Defenders as I can, then as many Midfielders as I can, and then as few Forwards as I can. Perhaps this formation will change as the season progresses, depending on whether relative points/cost changes between different positions. I also will use as a tiebreaker a preference to add players from teams not already in my squad, to hopefully reduce the variance of my weekly points.
Below, we’ll order players by the ratio of their points over the last two seasons, divided by their current cost. I’ll then select for my initial squad players with a high ratio and a low cost.The idea is that I’m happy to buy underpriced players who score fewer points, so that I have the flexibility later in the season to use current season data to make transfers. Currently, I’m picking based on prior season performance, which it feels fair to assume is uniformly a worse indicator for future performance than current season data.

title: GW 1: The Initial Squad
text:
Leftover Capital
This leaves me with £14m to play with. If I make 38 transfers over the season, I can average a net cost of ~£0.5m per transfer. The idea is that every transfer I make will use some capital to improve my team made from old data, on the basis of new data (current season data). I expect my initial squad to optimal with respect to the old data (as far as my selection logic is concerned), but to be a very poor predictor of this season’s performance when compared with current season data, as it eventually emerges. Selecting a cheap initial squad gives me flexiblity to leverage current season data to make “corrections” to my initial squad that was chosen from old data.

title: GW 2-6: The Warm Up
text:
Where to go from my initial squad?
I picked my initial squad based on past season points data and current price data. I obviously expect this team to not be the optimal team for this season - both because the past data will not be a completely accurate predictor for future performance, and because, even if it were, I don’t expect my crude points/cost metric to fully capture that putative predictive power. This makes sense for all players, amateur and experienced alike, otherwise transfers would not be such a limited resource.
Given that I know I will need to make transfers to improve my squad, and that I know the basis on which I picked that inital team is suboptimal, it follows that the basis on which I should make transfers as the season progresses is that points that players score in the current season. This is obvious. What requires more judgement is when to start making transfers. I’ll have current season data as soon as GW 1 has been played. Each player will have one datapoint for “points” the current season. Do I make a transfer based on that? Should I buy the player who scores the most points and sell my player who scores fewest? Making transfers based on one current data point (compared with the 38 * 2 = 76 datapoints for the iniital squad) seems ill-advised - that one datapoint is liable to noise. What I need to observe first is a burning-in period, a period long enough that the “currentness” (implicitly, predictive power) of the data is no longer outweighed by the volatility it carries by virtue of being much less than 76 data points.

title: GW 2-6: The Warm Up
text:
The burn-in period
In absence of any knowlegde of how long it takes players to warm up to the new season, and in balance of not wanting to wait too long, given my suboptimal initial squad, I’ll start making transfers after GW 6.

title: GW 2-6: The Warm Up
text:
Initial Squad performance
In the meantime, we can see how our initial squad fares.









Given my initial squad cost £86m, I expect it to underperform the average (hopefully only slightly). GW 2 was the only starkly different week to the average performance. I don’t want to read too much into the performance of my initial squad during the burn-in period, but the graph is fun to look at.

title: GW 7: The Game Begins
text:
Sample data
Now the burn-in period is complete, and I can start making transfers based on players’ recent points performance. Let’s have a look at a sample timeseries of points data for a random player: Benjamin White.

title: GW 7: The Game Begins
text:
Exponentially Weighted Moving Averages (EWMA)
I will be buying and selling players based on exponentially weighted moving averages (EWMA). An exponentially weighted moving average is different from a simple moving (or rolling) average in that it (exponentially) upweights more recent observations in the average calculation. The disadvantage of only using the most recent data point to inform my transfers is that I would often be making decisions based on noise. The disadvantage of using a simple moving average is that I am implicitly making older data as important as newer data in my calculation. The exponentially weighted moving average is a pragmatic halfway house that uses all the available data, but is less influenced by older data.

title: GW 7: The Game Begins
section: The Exponentially Weighted Moving Average Crossover (EWMAC)
text:
The Exponentially Weighted Moving Average Crossover (EWMAC)
The strategy I will be using is called an Exponentially Weighted Moving Average Crossover (EWMAC). Put simply, in addition to the criterion of having a high SMA, I will look to buy players whose short term EWMA is also higher than their long term EWMA. Conversely, I will look to sell any of my players whose short term EWMA is lower than their long term EWMA. The idea is that when a player’s short term EWMA is higher than their long term EWMA, their form is improving, and vice versa. Transgerring based on the crossover of a short and long term EWMA, rather than one EWMA means I should heopfully yuy (sell) players who not are in improving (deteriorating) form, but are in “accelerating” in that direction, rather than tapering off. This hopefully will cut out noise and save me from making transfers based on signals that soon stabilise.

Parameters
How do I do decide what short term and long term means in football? The alpha parameter in the EWMA formula defines the weight of the most recent observation i.e. 0.5 means that the most recent value will contribute to half od the EQMA value. The remaining points follow suit geometrically, so the second to last point contibutes half of the remaining weight, which makes a quarter, the third last point will contribute an eight to the average, etc. etc.
I will choose an alpha of a half for the short term EWMA, and an alpha of a quarter for the long term EWMA. If this proves too volatile, I’ll adjust this later. But this is something that I don’t want to adjust more than once or twice over the whole season.

title: GW 7: The Game Begins
text:
Computing EWMAC(0.5, 0.25)
Let’s go back to Benjamin White and compute his EWMA-0.5 and EWMA-0.25 as well as the crossover. We’ll also include his simple 4 week moving average (SMA-4) of points.









Both EWMAs smooth out the underlying timeseries. The short EWMA (alpha=0.5) being below the long EWMA (alpha=0.25) indicates that White’s form is only deteriorating. Note that we don’t get values for SMA-4 until we have 4 data points.

Joao Pedro

title: International Break
text:
Correlations
I’m using this break to investigate a thought, or worry, that occurred to me - is it generally a riskier idea to pick players from the same team? Will it make my points more volatile, based on the idea that scores for players in the same team might be more positively correlated?

title: International Break
text:
All correlations
First, let’s get every player’s points time series up to GW10, and get every single correlation of each player, with every other player.









Looks roughly normal with a bit of positive skew.


Intra-team correlations









Already this looks like there’s more of a bulge of mass on the positive side. This seems to support the hypothesis, but hard to say if this is significant without some kind of direct comparison.


Intra-position correlations









This just looks very similar to the “All correlations” histogram. I think that’s to be expected - why would we expect that e.g. midfielders all score particular similarly or particularly differently across different teams.


Intra-team-position correlations









Looks similar to the intra-team picture. Would we expect players in the same team and the same position to have correlated scores? Perhaps it depends on the position - defenders all get a clean sheet together, but only the scoring player gets the points (and is less likely to be a defender)

title: International Break
text:
Comparing correlations
It’s hard to compare whether correlations are different between the groups, so we’ll conduct some comparisons. We’ll normalise the histograms to account the different volumes, so that we’re only comparing their shapes.

Inter-team vs Intra-team









The blue peeking out on the right shows that players’ scores tend to be slightly more correlated with their teammates’, compared with players in other teams.


Inter-position vs Intra-position









Looks very insignificant.


Inter-position-team vs all correlations









This is interesting - the intra-position-team position is flatter and wider. This supports the clean-sheet X scorers observation that some correlations are very positive (clean sheets) and some are very negative (scorers). Let’s look at it more closely:


Intra-team correlations per position


Goalkeeper









This makes a lot of sense. Generally, between goalkeepers on the same team, only one of them will play so one will score at least 2, and the other will score probably nothing. So a negative correlation makes complete sense. This discussion is fairly redundant except as a sense check given you can only play one GK. Although perhaps it suggests that the safest way to ensure your GK scores at least 2 points is to have two GKs from the same team? Even this is a bit redundant because between two starting keepers, it seems unlikely that they both don’t play, so the additional likelihood is probably not worth the points differential between the sub keeper and the starting keeper from another team.


Defender









Defenders’ scores tend to be more positively correlated. Again, makes sense because all defenders receive or don’t receive the clean sheet together.


Midfielder









Probably nothing too significant here - a slight bias towards more negative correlation


Forward









A bit more of a bias towards negative skew here. Probably because goals are worth a lot of points and the most someone else gets is the assist.

title: International Break
text:
Conclusion
So what do I take from this?

Intra-team correlations are not categorically risky
I’m not concerned that the notion of having 3 players from one team is inherently risky. But:


Intra-team-position correlations can be risky or useful
Having multiple players from the same team and the same position can be a risk or an opportunity. Looking at the flatter Intra-position-team comparison graph, I need to choose pairs/triples that are negatively correlated, to minimise volatility. Based on what we see:

Goalkeepers from the same team tend to have negative correlated scores, but given that it seems very unlikely for two starting GKs from different teams to both not play, it’s probably not worth the cost of lower points expectations (from the sub keeper) in return a potentially lower volatility
Defenders on the same team have signficantly more positively correlated scores (compared with all correlations). I should be careful before selecting defenders from the same team - their sum is more likely to score very high or very low, whereas I would much rather something in the middle more reliably.
Midfielder intra-team-position correlations don’t bear much thought - their distribution is very similar to the all correlations distribution
(Good) Forwards from the same team is a good idea (compared with forwards from separate teams) because they tend to be more negatively correlated.
